narration.text: The planet travels around the Sun, spinning on a tilted axis.
That tilt, not its distance from the Sun, is what makes the seasons.
In summer, your side leans toward the Sun, and its light strikes the field directly.
The light falls on less ground, so the field warms more.
Months later, the same side leans away, and sunlight arrives at a slant.
The same light spreads thinner, so the ground stays cold, and that is winter.
In spring, the tilt leans neither toward the Sun nor away from it.
Then daylight lasts about half the day, at the equinox.

brief.title: Tilt, not distance, makes the seasons
brief.summary: Why summer and winter come from the planet's tilted axis, not from how near it is to the Sun.
